titre: A laser counted what a century of machete work had not seen
accroche: In 2018, a laser survey of the Petén reveals beneath the forest a Maya occupation far beyond what had been estimated
contenu_vulgarise:
Excavating beneath a dense tropical forest is slow work. You clear with a machete, record, advance a few dozen meters. A century of work in the Maya lowlands had produced a map made of scattered sites, separated by blank space.

That blank was not empty. It was forest that had not been opened up.

## Seeing through the trees

LiDAR reverses the relationship. An airplane sweeps the ground with a laser and measures the return time of each pulse.

Under forest cover, most pulses bounce off the leaves. But a fraction passes between them, reaches the ground, and comes back. All you have to do is keep only the latest returns, those that traveled farthest, to reconstruct the terrain stripped of vegetation.

This bare-earth model brings out what an archaeologist on the ground cannot perceive: alignments, platforms, embankments, regular depressions, that is, leveled and overgrown constructions.

## What the 2016 survey delivered

A campaign carried out in northern Guatemala swept more than two thousand square kilometers of Petén forest, the heart of Classic Maya civilization. The results appear in *Science* in 2018.

They count more than sixty thousand new structures. Causeways linking cities thought to be independent. Systems of terraces and canals covering considerable agricultural areas. And above all fortifications (ramparts, ditches, defensive works), far more numerous than expected.

The consequences go beyond the count. A population revised sharply upward means also revising the agriculture that fed it, hence the organization of labor, hence the nature of power. And the abundance of defenses runs against the long-prevailing image of ceremonial city-states not much given to war.

## What the instrument does not do

One point deserves to be held firmly, because media enthusiasm regularly erases it.

LiDAR dates nothing. It delivers a relief, not a chronology: two neighboring structures on the model can be separated by six centuries. Nor does it distinguish a monument from a pile of stones, or continuous occupation from abandonment followed by reoccupation.

Every interpretation remains dependent on ground probes, pottery, dating. The laser does not replace excavation: it tells it where to dig, and above all it finally provides a denominator, what has been excavated measured against what exists.

That may be the real contribution. For a century, Maya archaeology reasoned from a sample whose size it did not know.

repere.texte: The 2016 laser survey covered more than 2,000 km² of Petén forest and revealed more than 60,000 previously unknown structures, including causeways, agricultural terraces, and numerous fortifications.
repere.source: Canuto et al., “Ancient lowland Maya complexity as revealed by airborne laser scanning of northern Guatemala,” Science, 361, 2018

carte.punch: In a single flyover, a laser counted what a century of machete work had not seen.
carte.idee: Beneath the Petén forest, a laser scan revealed more than 60,000 previously unknown Maya structures: causeways, terraces, fortifications. For a century, archaeology had been reasoning from a sample whose size it did not know.

quiz.question: What can LiDAR not do?
choix: Detect structures entirely covered by vegetation
Cover, in a few days, areas inaccessible on foot
Spot leveled works that nothing signals on the ground
Establish what period the structures it reveals date from
quiz.explication: The laser reproduces a terrain stripped of vegetation: it excels at spotting what is buried or leveled, over vast areas and in little time. But a terrain model carries no chronological information. Two neighboring structures can be separated by several centuries, and only ground probes can settle it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does LiDAR work to reveal structures beneath the canopy?
choix: It detects the heat given off by buried stones
It keeps only the latest pulses, which reached the ground between the leaves
It analyzes the chemical composition of the soil by spectrometry
It compares aerial photographs taken in different seasons
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Under the canopy, most laser pulses bounce off the leaves, but a fraction passes between them and reaches the ground. By keeping only the latest returns, the terrain stripped of vegetation is reconstructed.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the LiDAR survey reveal, in addition to isolated structures?
choix: New glyphic inscriptions making it possible to date the cities
Organic remains making it possible to identify the inhabitants' diet
Obsidian tools, previously unknown in the region
Causeways linking cities thought to be independent, and numerous fortifications
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The survey of more than 2,000 km² delivered more than sixty thousand new structures: causeways linking cities thought to be independent, systems of terraces and canals, and fortifications far more numerous than expected.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why is LiDAR alone not enough to establish a chronology?
choix: Because tropical vegetation systematically skews height measurements
Because airplanes can fly over only a small part of the territory at a time
Because it reproduces only a relief, with no information about the age of the structures
Because only stone structures appear on the model, never wooden ones
quiz_supplementaire.explication: LiDAR delivers a relief, not a chronology: two neighboring structures on the model can be separated by six centuries. Only ground probes, pottery, and dating can settle between them.
